                            26   associated with time spent by other investigators. Id. ¶ 4.

                             7   will merely seek to recover the amount it spent investigating and remediating Folger’s illicit acts.

                             8          D.      Punitive Damages Further Increase the Amount in Controversy.

                             9          “It is well established that punitive damages are part of the amount in controversy in a

                            10   civil action.” Gibson v. Chrysler Corp., 261 F.3d 927, 945 (9th Cir. 2001), holding modified by

                            11   Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Servs., Inc., 545 U.S. 546 (2005). The Court may award Meta

                            12   damages if it holds the Section 502 violation was “willful” and finds Folger guilty “by clear and

                            13   convincing evidence” of “oppression, fraud, or malice as defined in subdivision (c) of Section

                            14   3294 of the Civil Code.” Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(4) (emphasis added). Meta alleged fraud,

                            15   Compl. ¶¶ 39, 51, and malice, id. ¶¶ 39–46, in substance. Cf. Cal. Civ. Code §§ 3294(c)(1),

                            17   amount in controversy.

                            19          As demonstrated above, the amount in controversy significantly exceeds $75,000. It is

  1                         MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES

 2   I.     PROCEDURAL HISTORY

 3          On February 18, 2025, Plaintiff META PLATFORMS, INC. (“Meta) filed its Complaint

 4   [ECF No. 1] against Folger, which alleges: 1) breach of contract; and 2) violation of the Computer

 5   Data Access and Fraud Act (“CDAFA”), California Penal Code § 502. The gravamen of the

 6   Complaint is that “Folger sold Instagram usernames and unauthorized Instagram account

 7   reinstatement services” with the intent “to circumvent enforcement actions taken by Meta in

 8   response to users who violate the Instagram Terms of Use…[and] Instagram’s Community

 9   Guidelines.” Id. at ¶ 1. Meta alleges diversity jurisdiction “pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1332 because

10   complete diversity between Meta and Defendant exists and because the amount in controversy

11   exceeds $75,000.” Id. at ¶ 6.

12   II.    STATEMENT OF FACTS

13          1.      On March 28, 2023, Meta sent a cease-and-desist letter to Folger, stating that it had

14   gathered unspecified evidence that Folger was “promoting and facilitating unauthorized account

15   support services such as reenabling access to disabled Instagram accounts…as well as offering to

16   sell and selling Instagram usernames for a profit.”        See Complaint at Ex. A; and Cristalli

17   Declaration at ¶ 3.

18          2.      On March 29, 2023, counsel for Folger sent a response to Meta’s counsel, denying

19   the allegations made in the cease-and-desist letter and requesting the opportunity to review the

20   evidence alluded to in the letter, with the goal of working towards a mutually acceptable resolution

21   of the issue. See Exhibit A; and Cristalli Declaration at ¶ 4.

22          3.      Counsel for Meta did not respond to the March 29 letter from Folger’s counsel and

23   did not attempt to communicate with Folger’s counsel regarding a potential pre-litigation

24   resolution. See Cristalli Declaration at ¶ 5.

25   III.   LEGAL ARGUMENT

26          A.      Legal Standard for Diversity Jurisdiction

27          Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a), “[t]he district courts shall have original jurisdiction of all

28   civil actions where the matter in controversy exceeds the sum or value of $75,000, exclusive


                                                 Page 3 of 10
  1   of interest and costs, and is between-- (1) citizens of different States…” (emphasis added). The

 2   determination of the value of the matter in controversy for purposes of federal jurisdiction is a

 3   federal question to be decided under federal standards, although federal courts must look to state

 4   law to determine the nature and extent of the right to be enforced in a diversity case. Horton v.

 5   Liberty Mut. Ins. Co. (1961) 367 U.S. 348, 352-353 [81 S.Ct. 1570, 1573, 6 L.Ed.2d 890] (citation

 6   omitted). The amount in controversy, for purpose of establishing diversity jurisdiction, includes

 7   any result of the litigation, excluding interests and costs, that entails a payment by the defendant,

 8   including compensatory damages, punitive damages, the cost of complying with an injunction, and

 9   attorney fees awarded under fee shifting statutes. Gonzales v. CarMax Auto Superstores, LLC (9th

10   Cir. 2016) 840 F.3d 644, 648-49 (citations omitted). Where the plaintiff originally files in federal

11   court, “the amount in controversy is determined from the face of the pleadings.” Geographic

12   Expeditions, Inc. v. Estate of Lhotka ex rel. Lhotka (9th Cir. 2010) 599 F.3d 1102, 1106 quoting

13   Crum v. Circus Circus Enterprises (9th Cir. 2000) 231 F.3d 1129, 1131.

14           B.      The Court Lacks Diversity Jurisdiction Given the Amount in Controversy.

15           While Meta (Delaware and California) and Folger (Nevada) are citizens of different states,

16   the amount in controversy does not exceed $75,000. While the Complaint vaguely references

17   compensatory damages, statutory damages, punitive damages, an injunction, and reasonable

18   attorney’s fees, Meta does not specify any amount(s) associated with such relief. Folger addresses

19   each of these items of relief in turn infra.

20                   1.      Compensatory Damages

21           As to its contract claim, Meta alleges “Defendant’s breaches have caused Meta to incur

22   damages, including damages attributable to the efforts and resources it used to investigate and

23   remediate Defendant’s conduct, in an amount to be proven at trial.” See Complaint at ¶ 53

24   (emphasis added). As to its statutory claim, Meta requests the same damages for “the expenditure

25   of resources to investigate and remediate Defendant’s conduct.” See Complaint at ¶ 61

26   (emphasis added). However, California adheres to the single satisfaction rule, whereby a plaintiff

27   is entitled to no more than a single recovery for each distinct item of compensable damages

28   supported by the evidence, regardless of the nature and number of legal theories advanced by the


                                                    Page 4 of 10
  1   plaintiff; double or duplicative recovery for the same items of damage amounts to prohibited

 2   overcompensation. Nada Pacific Corp. v. Power Eng'g and Mfg., Ltd. (N.D. Cal. 2014) 73

 3   F.Supp.3d 1206, 1218 citing Tavaglione v. Billings (1993) 4 Cal.4th 1150, 1158–1159 [17

 4   Cal.Rptr.2d 608, 614, 847 P.2d 574, 580], as modified (Apr. 28, 1993) (additional citation omitted).

 5   Thus, Meta is only entitled to a single recovery for its alleged compensatory damages, despite

 6   requesting it under both claims for relief. By extension, the Court can only consider compensatory

 7   damages once in calculating the actual amount in controversy.

 8                     2.       Punitive Damages

 9            Meta only references punitive damages in its prayer for relief. See Complaint at 15:7. In

10   California, a complaint must include specific factual allegations showing that defendant’s conduct

11   was oppressive1, fraudulent2, or malicious3 to support a claim for punitive damages. Today's IV,

12   Inc. v. Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (2022) 83 Cal.App.5th 1137

13   [300 Cal.Rptr.3d 61] (citation omitted). In other words, “[p]unitive damages may not be pleaded

14   generally.” Id. (emphasis added). While the relaxed federal pleading standards apply in a diversity

15   action, a plaintiff must still include a short and plain prayer for punitive damages that avers malice

16   or fraudulent intent, even if in an unsupported and conclusory fashion. Rees v. PNC Bank, N.A.

17   (N.D. Cal. 2015) 308 F.R.D. 266, 273.

18            Here, Meta does not allege that Folger acted with the requisite oppression, fraud, or malice

19   which would support a potential punitive damages award. See Complaint, generally. Under

20   California law, punitive damages are never available solely for a breach of contract claim, even

21   where the breach is intentional, willful, or in bad faith. Alberts v. Liberty Life Assurance Company

22   of Boston (N.D. Cal. 2014) 65 F.Supp.3d 790, 795. Under the CDAFA, punitive damages are

23   available “where it is proved by clear and convincing evidence that a defendant has been guilty of

24   oppression, fraud, or malice as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 3294 of the Civil Code.”

25
     1
       Oppression “means despicable conduct that subjects a person to cruel and unjust hardship in conscious disregard of
26   that person's rights.” Cal. Civ. Code, § 3294(c)(2).
     2
       Fraud “means an intentional misrepresentation, deceit, or concealment of a material fact known to the defendant
27   with the intention on the part of the defendant of thereby depriving a person of property or legal rights or otherwise
     causing injury.” Cal. Civ. Code, § 3294(c)(3).
28   3
       Malice “means conduct which is intended by the defendant to cause injury to the plaintiff or despicable conduct
     which is carried on by the defendant with a willful and conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others.” Cal. Civ.
     Code, § 3294(c)(1).

 4   consider punitive damages in calculating the actual amount in controversy.

 5                   3.      Statutory Damages

 6           Meta alleges a violation of California Penal Code § 502. A party bringing a civil action

 7   under Section 502(e) may only request compensatory damages, injunctive relief (or other equitable

 8   relief), reasonable attorney’s fees, and punitive or exemplary damages. § 502(e)(1), (2), (4). There

 9   are no other damages or civil penalties available. In short, there are no separate statutory damages

10   available to Meta. Thus, the Court cannot consider statutory damages in calculating the actual

11   amount in controversy.

12                   4.      Injunctive Relief

13           Meta also requests injunctive relief. See Complaint at ¶¶ 3, 54, 61, and 14:2-15:5. Under

14   either viewpoint rule, the test for determining the amount in controversy for purposes of diversity

15   jurisdiction is the pecuniary result to either party which the judgment would directly produce; in

16   other words, when the value of plaintiff’s potential recovery is below the jurisdictional amount,

17   but the potential cost to defendant of complying with the injunction exceeds that amount, it is the

18   latter that represents the amount in controversy for jurisdictional purposes. In re Ford Motor

19   Co./Citibank (South Dakota), N.A. (9th Cir. 2001) 264 F.3d 952, 958. “A request for injunctive

20   relief by itself, however, does not state a cause of action and is properly brought before the court

21   as a separate motion.” Fortaleza v. PNC Financial Services Group, Inc. (N.D. Cal. 2009) 642

22   F.Supp.2d 1012, 1028 (citation omitted). Moreover, even if a court construes a request for

23   injunctive relief as derivative of all other alleged causes of action, a plaintiff will still bear the

24   burden of showing: 1) a likelihood of success on the merits; 2) the likelihood of irreparable harm

25   in the absence of preliminary relief; 3) that the balance of equities tips in favor of an injunction;

26   and 4) that an injunction is in the public interest. Id.

27           Here, Meta has not filed a motion for injunctive relief. See Civil Docket for Case #: 3:25-

28   cv-01672-LB. Nor has Meta sufficiently plead injunctive relief, alleging only that it “has suffered


                                                  Page 6 of 10
  1   irreparable harm for which there is no adequate remedy at law.” See Complaint at ¶ 54. There are

 2   no allegations as to Meta’s likelihood of success, the balance of equities, or the public interest. Id.,

 3   generally. Thus, the Court should not consider any cost to Folger associated with injunctive relief

 4   in calculating the actual amount in controversy.

 5                    5.       Attorney Fees

 7   or discretionary language, such fees may be included in the amount in controversy.” Surber v.
